headline: A second job: replacing the audio in sessions that already exist
highlights: Replace Files is new and it deletes audio. Three things to know: an old take is only removed once every placement of it has been replaced, so a failed or stopped run keeps the files the session still plays; the files that landed are moved into “_ALREADY UPDATED IN THE SESSION” beside where they came from; and the replaced takes stay in Pro Tools' Clip List as “… OLD VERSION”, because its scripting has no way to remove them — Clip List → Select → Unused, then Clear, tidies that.

Replace Files, chosen on the first screen. Drop in the .ptx sessions and the new takes, and each clip keeps its track, its position and its name while the audio behind it changes. It runs through a batch of sessions one after another, saving and closing each one before the next is opened.

Nothing is replaced without a confirmed match. One file named exactly as a clip is a match; two files answering to one name, or a clip nobody sent a file for, arrive in the preview as a question and are left exactly as they are until you answer it. Case and extension are ignored, and so is the “-01” Pro Tools adds to keep clip names unique.
The preview lists every clip each session holds and the file that will replace it, so the whole run can be checked before anything is touched. A clip can be assigned a file by hand, or left alone.

What happens to the take that was replaced is yours to choose: backed up beside the session and then removed, removed outright, or left where it is. The backup is made before the deletion, and a backup that fails stops its file being deleted.

Session folders can be cleared out: the waveform cache, the folder of auto-saves, and anything else that is not the session, its Audio Files or its Video Files. It shows every entry it would remove with its size, and marks renders, bounces and fades as audio that cannot be recreated — and removes nothing until you say so.

A replace run cross-checks itself against the session afterwards, the same way a build does, and says where the new media actually landed: inside the session's Audio Files, or merely referenced where it lies.

A TC Check REF track. Under each percentage-constrained line it lays a blank region running from the shortest that take may be to the longest — a 60-second reference at TC 10% gives a 12-second window, opening at 54 seconds and closing at 66. Computed in whole samples, never in seconds. It sits below the muted repeats where a session has them, and below the reference clip where it does not.

The TC Check REF window sits under the clip you choose: the muted repeat by default, since that is the slot being worked into, or the main clip. A session with no repeats uses the main clip either way.

A Subtract Track: a region wherever the takes are not, from the start of the session to the end. You choose whether the negative is taken from the reference takes, the muted repeats or both, and whether it goes in the session or in a session of its own.

The muted repeat can be its own duplicated clip, named with the “__muted” suffix, instead of a second placement of the same one. On by default, because Pro Tools names a clip rather than a placement of it, so a shared repeat can only wear its reference's name. Sharing is still there as the alternative: one file, one import, nothing extra in the session.

Both new tracks are drawn in the preview as what they are — their own colour, their own label, and a line in the track header saying what the regions are for — instead of reading as a track of takes that all failed to import. They are not counted as missing takes, and they are counted as the blank files they really are on disk.

Recalling a memory location no longer hides tracks. The markers this tool creates were carrying a track-visibility property, so recalling one changed what was visible in the session — a marker is a position, and it should not rearrange the session around it.

Any TC percentage is recognised, not just 10% and 20%: TC 5%, TC 15%, TC 7% and the rest all resolve to a constraint with its own colour. TC 0% is read as strict, and a label the library has never seen can still be kept as a type of its own.

Extra tracks can carry a note each — written beside the track in the panel, or pasted as “TRACK NAME | the note”. Pro Tools' scripting API has no field a build can write on a track itself, so each note is written as a memory location at the session start, named after its track.

The options panel is regrouped, one concern per card: missing takes are their own card instead of sitting inside the line pattern, clip colour leaves the markers card, the TC Check REF and Subtract tracks get a Reference tracks card of their own, and extra tracks go last.

Clicking a panel card opens the card you are pointing at. The click is now taken from where the pointer is rather than from where the window reports it, which is the same reading the highlight uses — so what lights up and what opens are always the same card.

Replace Files works. Nothing on that screen was watching the Pro Tools connection, so its status stayed “unknown” for ever and every button on it stayed disabled — dropping a session in appeared to do nothing at all. It also no longer waits for a session to be open in Pro Tools, which was the wrong thing to wait for: it opens the sessions you give it.

The replacement files are listed one by one, each removable, with the folder each came from beside it — two takes of the same line in two folders is the usual way a delivery goes wrong. Sessions and files clear separately, so a wrong folder of takes does not cost you the session list.

The pointer no longer lands slightly off what it is pointing at in the options panel. It was never the pointer: almost every caption in there sized itself to its own text, and those captions change with the setting above them — so switching one moved every row below it, and the next click landed on whatever had slid underneath. Captions now reserve their space, rows that used to appear and disappear stay put and disable instead, the progress bar is pinned under the panel rather than pushed in above the cards — and when something does legitimately move, and hover no longer depends on macOS delivering an enter or an exit event for every row: the panel tracks where the pointer is and each row works out whether it is under it, so a row that moves — because the panel scrolled, or re-laid itself out — is right immediately.

A line with no audio and a TC Check REF window no longer shares one blank file between them. They are different lengths, and the window — the one clip whose whole purpose is to be exactly the right length — was being handed the stand-in take's file.

A build now cross-checks itself. When it finishes, the session is asked to describe itself — Pro Tools' own session export, with every clip's position in samples — and that is compared against the plan: clips missing from where they were planned, clips at the right position under another name, tracks that never appeared, and anything sitting on one of the build's own tracks that was never planned. Until now a build could only report what it sent, which is a different question from whether the session is right.

Typing in the session name, track name, extra prefix or any gap no longer replans the whole session on every keystroke. The fields hand over what you typed when it settles — or at once on Return, on leaving the field, or on a stepper click — so the lag between pressing a key and seeing the character is gone.
NLT is recognised as a time constraint. Its name is the code itself for now, because nobody here invented an expansion for it.

A time-constraint label the library does not know can be kept as a type of its own with a name, instead of being filed under one of the built-in six that it is not. The library remembers both the type and the label that produced it.
Clip colours by time constraint are yours to choose: the panel lists the types this session actually contains, and a colour set there reaches the preview, the menus and the clips Pro Tools builds.
